value: It is a problem when PAGEIOLATCH_SH and WRITELOG each take at least 30 % of the wait delta and are at least 100 ms per task worse than the reference hour. Here they reached 44% and 31%, at +124 ms and +104 ms per task.
Compare Incident share with Reference share: PAGEIOLATCH_SH rose from 14% to 44% and WRITELOG from 9% to 31%, both past 30 %. Per-task deltas are +124 ms and +104 ms, both past 100 ms, so it is real.

Left half is the reference hour, right half the incident hour; no marker line is drawn here. Each band is one wait type, sized by its share of wait time in percent. A thicker band means a bigger share.
A healthy chart looks like this one: SLEEP_TASK makes up 62% of the wait delta (the new wait time) and LAZYWRITER 22%. These are normal background waits, not signs of trouble.

Compare the Delta share and Delta ms per task columns in the table: a problem needs a bottleneck wait at 30% or more of the delta and 100 ms per task worse. Here PAGEIOLATCH_SH is 3% and 0.9 ms, so it is fine.

Left half is the normal reference hour, right half the incident hour; no marker line is drawn here. Each band is one wait type: SLEEP_TASK, LAZYWRITER, PAGEIOLATCH_SH. A thicker band means a bigger share.

value.d: a normal wait when a background task is idle, waiting for its next job.
a background job that writes old data out of memory to make room.
a wait for a shared read of a data page from disk or memory.
millisecond, one thousandth of a second.

value: Compare each query's p95 ms in the table to the 400 ms limit: if every query stays under 400 ms, it passes the hard limit, like here. The 30% and 100 ms comparison needs the reference duration, which this card does not show.
Left half is the reference hour, right half the incident hour. Each bar is the p95 duration in ms for the Orders.Create query; the incident bars are highlighted. A taller bar means a slower query.
Compare the LCK_M_X delta ms in the table to the watch marks (at least 15% and 50 ms per task worse than reference). Whether any session is queued is shown on the blocking card, not this one.
Left half is the reference hour, right half the incident hour; no marker line is drawn here. Each band is one lock wait type (LCK_M_S, LCK_M_X, LCK_M_IX). A thicker band means more wait time.
Compare each job's Overlap min in the table to the incident window; then look at the wait-type cards for a spike at the same time. Here the overlap is real but no wait lines up with it.
Left half is the reference hour, right half the incident hour. Each bar is a maintenance job running in that window; the incident bars are highlighted. A taller bar means more overlap minutes.

It is a problem when the head blocker is itself stuck on a lock (LCK_M_*) or a disk read (PAGEIOLATCH_*) for a long time. Here head blocker spid 61 waits on PAGEIOLATCH_SH; spid 78 and spid 84 wait behind it for 61 and 54 seconds.
Each bar is one session; a taller bar means more seconds spent blocked. The reference hour is the left half, the incident hour the right half, and the incident bars are highlighted.

value.d: a session ID, the number naming one connection to the database
a wait for an exclusive lock, needed to change a row or page
a pause while SQL Server reads a data page from disk
the one session at the front of a line of stuck sessions
a wait to access a page tempdb uses to track free space
SQL Server's shared scratch database used for temporary work
a tempdb page that tracks which pages are free or full
a tempdb page that tracks shared extents of space that still have room

value: Before MongoDB lets an operation touch stored data, it needs a ticket from a fixed pool (128 for reads and 128 for writes by default; this card tracks one pool of 128). When all are used, new operations wait in line.

WiredTiger gives each running read or write a ticket from a fixed pool (128 per direction by default; this card tracks one pool of 128). Tickets out is how many are in use. When almost all are taken, others wait, like a car park with no free spaces.

Two stacked bands: readers waiting below, writers on top, in average operations. Left half is the normal hour, right half the incident hour. No marker line is drawn; look for the writer band getting thicker.
Stacked area in percent. Left half is the reference hour, right half the incident hour; no marker line is drawn. The band is CPU used (user+sys); taller means busier.
Reference hour about 62% CPU; green means staying under 70%. Incident at 76% is above the amber start but below the red line (90% or more for 5 minutes).
Stacked area in percent. Left is the reference hour, right is the incident hour; no marker line is drawn. The band is CPU used (user+sys); taller means busier.

The Retransmits column says not collected in both rows, so this card alone cannot confirm impact. A helper can run the free command netstat -s, which counts how often network data had to be sent again.
Left half is the reference hour (a normal day), right half is the incident hour; no marker line is drawn. The shaded area is CPU used (user+sys), in percent of host CPU; taller means busier.

It is a real problem when the host thrashes, swapping heavily, or a process is killed for running out of memory (an OOM kill). Here available memory falls to 0.2 GB, swap out reaches about 1,300 pages per second, and 1 OOM kill is recorded.
